query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding ductile phase-forming elements, such as Cu or Al, to the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy will improve its integrity without sacrificing its caloric response.
generation.intervention: Adding ductile phase-forming elements (e.g., Cu, Al) to the alloy composition
generation.conditions: Applied-field and pressure-field operation, various temperatures and loading regimes
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a ductile phase within the alloy matrix
generation.mechanism: The added ductile phase-forming elements will enhance the alloy's toughness and reduce its tendency to crack, thereby improving its integrity. This is expected to occur without significantly compromising the alloy's caloric response, as the added elements will not substantially alter the alloy's magnetic or thermal properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved integrity, reduced cracking tendency, and retained high caloric response
generation.baseline: The original (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy with poor integrity and tendency to crack
generation.boundary: The alloy's operating conditions, including applied-field, pressure-field, temperature, and loading regimes
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of ductile phase-forming elements required to achieve the desired improvement in integrity without sacrificing caloric response is uncertain and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy samples with varying amounts of added ductile phase-forming elements (e.g., Cu, Al). Test the samples' integrity, caloric response, and microstructure using techniques such as scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and calorimetry.
measurements: Caloric response (e.g., magnetic entropy change, latent heat)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of ductile phase-forming elements does not improve the alloy's integrity or significantly compromises its caloric response, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). AbstractHigh-entropy alloys have gained widespread concern in response to the increased requirements for future high-temperature structural superalloys. By combining phase-diagram calculations with microhardness, compression behavior measurements at room temperature, and elevated temperature conditions, the very important role of the Cr element on the microstructure and properties is deeply revealed, which provides candidates materials for future high-temperature alloy applications. The increment of Cr favors the regulation of the two-phase fraction and distribution. The thermodynamic calculations illustrate that the density and melting point of the HEAs showed an increasing trend with the increase of the Cr content. The typical worm-like microstructure of the Cr0.6 alloy with a dual BCC structure was detected. Meanwhile, on the one hand, the increment of the Cr elements results in a considerable optimization of the mechanical properties of the alloy in terms of strength and ductility at room temperature. AbstractThe high-entropy transition metal borides containing a random distribution of five or more constituent metallic elements offer novel opportunities in designing materials that show crystalline phase stability, high strength, and thermal oxidation resistance under extreme conditions. We present a comprehensive theoretical and experimental investigation of prototypical high-entropy boride (HEB) materials such as (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti)B2 and (Hf, Mo, Nb, Ta, Zr)B2 under extreme environments of pressures and temperatures. The theoretical tools include modeling elastic properties by special quasi-random structures that predict a bulk modulus of 288 GPa and a shear modulus of 215 GPa at ambient conditions. HEB samples were synthesized under high pressures and high temperatures and studied to 9.5 GPa and 2273 K in a large-volume pressure cell. The thermal equation of state measurement yielded a bulk modulus of 276 GPa, in excellent agreement with theory. The measured compressive yield strength by radial X-ray diffraction technique in a diamond anvil cell was 28 GPa at a pressure of 65 GPa, which is a significant fraction of the shear modulus at high pressures.
